revisions.body: The argument’s key move is to turn poetic imagery into a test of habitat. Ate’s soft feet become a model for Eros, who both walks and dwells in the softest beings—characters and souls, avoiding hard dispositions. Agathon then infers fluid form from Eros’s supposed ability to envelop, enter, and leave souls unnoticed. The catalogue thus treats function as evidence for an attribute.

The ending makes form part of the performance. Agathon explicitly shifts into meter for a compact image of Eros as the maker of peace among humans and calm at sea, then labels the speech a mixture of play and measured seriousness. That label does not settle whether the praise is playful or serious; it asks the audience to hear both registers at once.

Socrates does not set Agathon’s encomium aside; he turns its picture of Eros into the material of the questioning. Agathon supplies the agreements: Eros is love of something, desire reaches toward what is lacking, and what is already possessed is not desired as such. The healthy person’s apparent counterexample is absorbed by shifting desire from present possession to continued presence in the future. The pressure therefore comes from Agathon’s own assent, while the target remains the beautiful Eros his speech had presented.

The reversal is now explicit. Socrates has Agathon recall his own claim that Eros loves beauty; then the agreed rule that love reaches toward what it lacks turns that claim against Eros. Agathon’s admission of ignorance marks the collapse of the earlier encomium, and the next inference extends the lack from beauty to good things because Agathon accepts that good things are beautiful. The exchange does not yet offer a positive definition of Eros; it shows how assent can expose the cost of a claim.

The earlier general rule now has a later target. Compare 201a–201b, where Socrates asks Agathon to retrieve his own description of Eros as love of beauty and tests it against the agreed principle that love concerns what one lacks. The turn from general premise to self-implication is the point to carry forward.

crossrefs.note: Socrates turns the agreed account of desire and lack against Agathon’s own description of Eros as love of beauty.
